title: National Security Commission on Robotics for Advanced Manufacturing (NSCRAM) Preliminary Report
page_note: "p." is the printed page number. Links open the PDF at that page (PDF page = printed page + 1).

themes.name: Deployment gap
themes.description: U.S. leads in AI and design but trails China in installations, stock and diffusion; deployment volume drives learning, cost and supplier investment.

themes.name: Components and supply chain
themes.description: Concentration in magnets, reducers, sensors and sub-tier parts, opaque supplier visibility, and cyber exposure from foreign-linked hardware.

themes.name: SME adoption barriers
themes.description: Small and medium manufacturers face capital, knowledge, readiness, ROI-framing and demand-signal barriers; RaaS and MEP help but are limited.

themes.name: Workforce and talent
themes.description: Aging workforce, lost wage premium, skills mismatch, apprenticeship limits, micro-credentials and STEM pipeline; employment effects are ambiguous.

themes.name: Federal coordination and public trust
themes.description: Fragmented agencies without a single accountable owner, ended programs, and contested public attitudes toward automation.

themes.name: Standards, safety and cybersecurity
themes.description: Safety, performance and liability standards lag flexible robots; networked systems expand attack surface; FCC Covered List action.

themes.name: Data and simulation
themes.description: Robot training data is scarce, proprietary and fragmented; simulation needs real-world grounding; China pays to pool data.

themes.name: Capital, financing and cost
themes.description: Venture timelines mismatch hardware; humanoids absorb funding, while China's deployment scale and supplier clusters affect costs.

findings.title: The US is not on track to lead physical AI at scale
findings.report_heading: Physical AI at scale will define the next industrial era, and the United States is not on a trajectory to lead it.
findings.summary: The US has the strongest AI models, research and startups, but builds and installs far fewer robots than China, makes few of the key parts, and few small factories use robots. The report measures leadership by robots at work, not by models.

evidence.claim: In 2024 the U.S. ranked eighth in robot density at roughly 307 robots per 10,000 manufacturing employees versus Korea's 1,220.
evidence.underlying_source: IFR, Robot Density Surges in Europe, Asia, and Americas (2026)

evidence.claim: China installed about 354,200 industrial robots in 2025 (59% of world installs) versus about 38,400 in the U.S.
evidence.underlying_source: IFR, China Installs 59 Percent of World's Industrial Robots (2026)

evidence.claim: Chinese suppliers held 55% of installations in their home market in 2025.
By end-2024 China had over two million operating industrial robots, more than five times the U.S. stock of 393,700.
evidence.underlying_source: IFR, China Tops World Record of 2 Million Factory Robots (2025)

evidence.claim: Share of U.S. establishments with active robots rises from 1.6% (0-5 employees) to 40.9% (1,000+); all establishments 6.4% (2022).
evidence.underlying_source: IFR / Census data as charted in Figure 2

findings.title: Buyers wait for cheaper robots; costs fall only with volume
findings.report_heading: A supply-demand paradox is preventing the U.S. robotics flywheel from starting.
findings.summary: Manufacturers hold off until robots get cheaper and easier to install. Robot makers can't cut costs until they sell more. Each side waits on the other, and small manufacturers are hit hardest.

evidence.claim: Regional robot adoption correlates with the presence of integrators and peer robot-using manufacturers (Census Annual Survey of Manufactures research).
evidence.underlying_source: Brynjolfsson et al., Robot Hubs in U.S. Manufacturing, Census (2023)

evidence.claim: NIST found small and medium manufacturers often lack robotics expertise, knowledge of capabilities, and unbiased guidance.
evidence.underlying_source: NIST, Best Practices for Cobot Integration in SMMs (2021)

findings.title: Federal programs are scattered and public trust is weak
findings.report_heading: Fragmented institutions, unmanaged strategic risk, and weak public confidence compound to block coordinated action.
findings.summary: Robotics programs sit in at least four federal departments with no one in charge. Many Americans worry about job losses. Foreign parts and software in US robots create supply and security risks.

evidence.claim: The National Robotics Initiative coordinated more than $250 million across more than 300 projects before NSF ended it in 2022.
July 2026 poll of 1,306 U.S. adults: 74% worried robots would take others' jobs within five years; 31% of 582 employed worried about their own job.
Comfort with robots: 63% in grocery stockrooms/loading docks, 59% cleaning floors, 39% at self-checkout.
Pittsburgh Robotics Network survey of 642 adults: 44% expect more U.S. manufacturing from robotics; 62% prefer or are more likely to use domestic robotics.
In 2024 Chinese-owned manufacturers held 57% of China's home industrial-robot market.
In 2024 China had about 60% of rare-earth mine production for magnets, 91% of refined output, and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production.
A 2026 robot-vacuum vulnerability exposed camera, audio and floor plans of nearly 7,000 devices in 24 countries.

findings.title: The effect on jobs is mixed and not settled
findings.report_heading: The effects of robotics on employment are ambiguous and not predetermined.
findings.summary: Robots remove some jobs, change others and create new ones, all at once. Studies disagree on the net effect, which depends on how fast robots spread and on policy. Recent factory job losses came mostly from the business cycle and trade.

evidence.claim: One welding developer reports a trained welder in a robotic cell can reach up to five times manual output.
evidence.underlying_source: SCSP staff engagement with Path Robotics (Aug 2026)

evidence.claim: U.S. commuting-zone study (1990-2007): each additional robot per thousand workers cut national employment by about 3.3 jobs.
Contrasting studies: zero net job loss across 17 industrialized countries; net positive effect across 16 EU economies.
U.S. manufacturing employment fell about 290,000 from 12.87M (Dec 2023) to 12.58M (Dec 2025); recovered 72,000 to 12.65M in Sept 2026.
Manufacturing job openings were 522,000 in August 2026, up from 416,000 a year earlier.

findings.title: Labor shortages and skills gaps limit deployment
findings.report_heading: Labor shortages and skills misalignment limit manufacturing at scale and robotics deployment.
findings.summary: Factory workers are getting older, factory pay no longer beats other work by much, and training is slow and scattered. The report points to short credentials, apprenticeships and hands-on engineering courses.

evidence.claim: Manufacturers need to fill about 3.8 million jobs by 2033, with up to 1.9 million possibly unfilled; 65% of executives cite talent as top challenge.
Median age in manufacturing is 44 versus 42.1 for all U.S. workers; 40% of manufacturing jobs are at firms where at least one in four workers is 55+.
Welding: over 157,000 welders (43%) retire within 15-20 years; about 80,000 openings per year 2025-2029.
Apprentices are 0.3% of the U.S. workforce; 95,000-97,500 registered manufacturing apprentices (about 0.7-0.8% in-training ratio).
evidence.underlying_source: Jobs for the Future (2025); DOL Office of Apprenticeship (2025)

evidence.claim: DOL awarded a four-year $35.8 million apprenticeship incentive fund paying $3,500 per apprentice completing 90 days.
evidence.underlying_source: Arkansas Office of Skills Development; NC Community Colleges

evidence.claim: U.S. fourth- and eighth-grade TIMSS math scores fell 18 and 27 points between 2019 and 2023.
57% of U.S. high schools offer computer science but only 5.8% of students enroll.

findings.title: AI programming and mobile robots are widening what can be automated
findings.report_heading: The industrial robotics landscape is undergoing a transformation in deployment dynamics driven by AI-assisted programming, low-code interfaces, and open-space mobile manipulation.
findings.summary: AI-assisted programming, simpler interfaces and mobile robots let smaller factories automate low-volume work. Safety and liability rules haven't caught up. Renting robots as a service lowers the upfront cost.

evidence.claim: Legacy standards do not fully cover AI-adaptive or dynamically balancing systems; humanoids need power to stay upright, so emergency shutdown can be hazardous.
evidence.underlying_source: Robey et al., Science (2026); MIT Technology Review (2025)

findings.title: Small manufacturers lack know-how, staff and steady demand
findings.report_heading: Robotics adoption across manufacturing remains constrained by lack of knowledge, internal capability gaps, and unsteady demand signals.
findings.summary: Many small manufacturers don't know what robots can do, lack the staff and IT to run them, and judge them on narrow payback numbers. Help programs like MEP are thin, and uneven orders make investment risky.

evidence.claim: MEP Centers are the primary federal vehicle for assisting SMMs but have limited resources and have faced proposed elimination.
The report identifies four reinforcing adoption barriers: financial, readiness, risk and liability, and knowledge gap.

findings.title: US robot makers face higher costs and a financing gap
findings.report_heading: Systematic cost disadvantages and a financing gap keep U.S. robotics firms from scaling production.
findings.summary: Venture funding suits software, not the tooling, inventory and field service hardware needs. US robot makers depend on Chinese sub-suppliers they often can't see, and humanoid startups get a large share of the money.

evidence.claim: Chinese makers collectively hold over 60% of China's domestic harmonic-reducer market; Leaderdrive has capacity exceeding 500,000 units a year.
China controls about 90% of rare-earth processing and 69% of mining; Chinese share of humanoid inputs: bearings 40%, motors 35%, power electronics 30%.
China's 2022 machine-tool output was $27.1B, about 4.6 times U.S. output of $5.9B.
Onboarding a new electronics manufacturer takes 12-20 weeks to first-article approval; stable volume takes four to six months.
Only 6.2% of 2,805 surveyed organizations had full visibility into Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers.
evidence.underlying_source: Achilles Annual Risk and Sustainability Report (2026)

evidence.claim: Physical AI VC deal count and volume nearly doubled from Q1 2024 to Q1 2026; humanoids took over 20% of funding with 3% of firms.
evidence.underlying_source: PitchBook, Robotics & Physical AI VC Trends (2026)

findings.title: Components and training data are bottlenecks
findings.report_heading: Supply chain bottlenecks for physical components and data keep U.S. robotics too expensive and too static.
findings.summary: Robot training data is locked in incompatible proprietary systems, and simulation can't fully replace it. China's scale, nearby suppliers and subsidies make parts cheaper. Integration, more than hardware, drives what a deployment costs.

evidence.claim: Open X-Embodiment pooled 60 datasets from 34 labs, 22 robot types, 527 skills, about one million trajectories.
China installed 295,000 industrial robots in 2024 (54% of world); domestic firms took 57% of home market, up from about 28% a decade ago.
One FANUC-certified integrator puts the robot at roughly a quarter of total cell cost.
Subsidies accounted for as much as 40% of net profit at some publicly listed Chinese robotics firms in some years.
China manufactures 94% of the world's permanent magnets.

findings.title: The Commission calls for a national mission built around deployment
findings.report_heading: A national mission is needed to start the U.S. robotics flywheel.
findings.summary: The report calls for a national strategy aimed at putting robots to work, with much more US hardware production. It says the US should not try to make every part at home or copy China's state-directed model.

evidence.claim: Proposed success measures: adoption breadth, time and cost from assessment to operation, pilot-to-repeat share, domestic and allied component capacity, integration services, workforce advancement, security and interoperability.

directions.text: The final report, due March 2027, will make recommendations to federal, state and regional officials, industry, educators, workers and investors.
This report diagnoses the problem. The recommendations come later.
The US should build much more robot hardware at home, without trying to make every part here.
Government should not pick one technology or copy China's state-directed model.
Government's job: set national goals, fix coordination problems, and remove barriers no single firm can.
Policy should aim at getting robots into productive use. Programs that don't do that miss the main problem.
Copying China's low-cost supply chain for older parts won't work. Designing around chokepoints might, for example motors that don't need rare earths.
Measure success by results: how many firms adopt robots, how long and how much it takes, how many pilots turn into repeat orders, and parts capacity. Not by program counts or dollars spent.
Public trust needs clear safety and workforce plans, a say for workers, training and accountability.
Better data on mobile robots and humanoids is needed before broader conclusions about who leads.
Safety standards for flexible robots and workforce credentials both need updating.

quotes.text: Physical AI at scale will define the next industrial era, and the United States is not on a trajectory to lead it.
Waiting for perfect technology or perfect evidence is not a neutral position. It is itself a strategic choice.
The United States cannot secure or scale a supply chain it cannot see.
Industrial data is abundant in aggregate and inaccessible in practice.

caveats.text: The report gives Chinese makers' share of China's market as 55% for 2025 here, and 57% for 2024 on pp. 26 and 67. Both are shown with their year.

Figure 2's China density of 166 robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers agrees with IFR's April 8, 2026 release for 2024. IFR revised China's workforce denominator using updated labor data. The older 470 figure covered 2023 on the earlier basis; these figures do not establish a comparable fall in robot adoption.
The humanoid share of robotics venture funding is "more than 20%" on p. 64 and "roughly 22%" in the appendix (p. 82).
This is a preliminary diagnosis. The Commission's recommendations are due in the final report in March 2027.
